cl_gen_deaths_autopsy_testing.q: Do autopsies and drug tests change which deaths count as drug deaths?
cl_gen_deaths_autopsy_testing.short: At one US centre, autopsies and drug tests changed the cause, both ways.
cl_gen_deaths_autopsy_testing.but: This rests on one autopsy centre in North Carolina; elsewhere, testing differs a lot.
how: At one autopsy centre in North Carolina (2016 to 2021), investigators suspected 2,719 deaths were drug deaths. After a full autopsy and drug tests, about 1 in 10 had another cause, such as a blood clot or a burst blood vessel in the brain.

That 1 in 10 is an upper limit, and only for the suspected deaths, because it includes deaths where the tests found no drug. Of 237 deaths nobody suspected, drug tests showed that about half were drug deaths.
In 2018, about 1 in 9 US death investigation offices said they had no access to drug testing (some may send deaths elsewhere), and small offices had it less often than big ones.
Medical examiners' guidance says to do an autopsy whenever a drug death is suspected, but its error figure comes mostly from autopsy studies of all kinds of deaths.

freq.what: of deaths suspected to be drug deaths had another cause after a full autopsy

cl_gen_deaths_who_investigates.q: Does it matter whether a coroner or a medical examiner investigates?
cl_gen_deaths_who_investigates.short: Not clear. Coroner areas recorded deaths less precisely, but switching showed no clear change.
cl_gen_deaths_who_investigates.but: No study checked which records were right, and the study of switching used data up to 1998.
how: In the US, medical examiners are usually doctors appointed to the job. Coroners are often elected, and in some states need no medical training.

In nine US states (2019 to 2021), deaths in coroner areas were more often recorded without saying whether the death was an accident or a suicide than deaths in medical examiner areas of the same state.
Other US studies found that death certificates named no drug more often where coroners work.
But seven states that switched to medical examiners showed no clear change in how precisely poisoning deaths were recorded, although that study could not rule out a real improvement.

cl_gen_deaths_news_stigma.q: Does how the news describes a drug death change what readers think?
cl_gen_deaths_news_stigma.short: In one study, story details changed how harshly readers judged the person who died.
cl_gen_deaths_news_stigma.but: Readers saw one made-up story and answered straight away; nobody checked what they did later.
how: In 2022, 1,248 adults in the UK each read one made-up news story about a drug death, with the details chosen at random.
Readers judged the person more harshly when the person was a man, was older and had used the drug for years, or had taken heroin rather than ecstasy. The differences were small to moderate.
Support for services that reduce harm, such as drug checking, barely changed.
The study could not tell the effect of age apart from the effect of using the drug for longer.

cl_cath_deaths_news_mephedrone.q: Did news stories about mephedrone deaths get the facts right?
cl_cath_deaths_news_mephedrone.short: Not always: several deaths blamed on it in the news had other causes.
cl_cath_deaths_news_mephedrone.but: One study, and the later test results are second-hand reports, not official records.
how: In 2009 and 2010, online news in the UK linked 18 named deaths to mephedrone.
Later reports said mephedrone was not found in 4, was found but did not cause the death in 4, and played a part in 7, mostly together with other drugs or illnesses.
The two deaths most linked to mephedrone online were later found to be from alcohol and methadone.
Online searches for mephedrone rose when deaths were in the news. The author thinks the news raised interest in the drug, but search data cannot show that the news made people use it.
